claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been reported in a hierarchical heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A transformer-based, physics-informed model integrating reduced-order multi-fidelity descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model will be more accurate and efficient than CALPHAD and first-principles methods.
Transformer pre-training on extensive synthetic materials data followed by fine-tuning on HEA data can mitigate limited experimental data.
Binary-alloy datasets are suitable pre-training data for the proposed HfNbTiVAl10 model.
Reduced-order local stress and strain fields can serve as informative descriptors for this alloy’s mechanical response.
Local chemical-order descriptors can capture the multilevel chemical fluctuations of the HfNbTiVAl10 hierarchical heterostructure.
Reduced-order descriptors can represent both elastic-regime behavior and fracture-zone evolution in the hierarchical structure.
Transformer self-attention can capture intricate elemental interactions relevant to macroscopic mechanical properties.
Physics-informed loss functions based on simulation outputs will enable the model to learn interactions governing elastic properties and fracture processes.
The proposed model will reduce RMSE for the three mechanical properties by approximately 30–50% relative to prior methods.
The proposed model will reduce computational cost by nearly one order of magnitude relative to prior methods.
The largest predictive-accuracy gains will occur for fracture toughness.
Ab initio and molecular-dynamics calculations are too time-consuming for high-throughput alloy-structure prediction.
CALPHAD can require significant computing resources and can be limited by the absence of reliable HEA databases.
Transformer models can outperform random forests and Gaussian processes for some HEA mechanical properties.
Existing HEA property-prediction work focuses mainly on yield strength or hardness rather than fracture toughness.
The proposed model will become unreliable when phase transitions, precipitate formation, or other microstructural evolution falls substantially outside the training distribution.
